inputs.original_text: Any political transition in Cuba must be judged by whether ordinary people gain real power—not by how quickly wealthy diaspora buyers and foreign investors can acquire land and businesses. When people already facing poverty and limited property have little say, privatization risks turning their labor and home into assets for those with the deepest pockets. Residents’ rights to own, work, and shape their future must come first; otherwise, political change could simply replace one unequal arrangement with another.
inputs.modified_text: The real test of any political transition in Cuba is whether ordinary people gain democratic control over their lives—not whether investors and wealthy buyers get first access to land and businesses. If people living with poverty and limited property are shut out of decisions, privatization can turn their homes and labor into opportunities for those who already have the most money. Any change that leaves residents without secure rights to own, work, and shape their future is not liberation; it risks preserving inequality under a new arrangement.
